EmbedEmbed<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6010647/nx-s1-mx-6010647-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Sometimes the hardest part about talking to other people isn'tfindingthe right words to say — butdecidingif you should say anything at all, says social psychologist Vanessa Bohns.
"There are times when honesty is the best policy," she says. "On the other hand, honesty isnotthe best policy if whatever we say is going to be honest without any instrumental value."
Bohns is the author ofShould I Say Something? The Science of What to Share—and What to Keep to Yourself, published in October. The book provides research-backed strategies to help you figure out when to share the truth or a personal opinion. It also offers advice on when to share good news, say sorry or be vulnerable.
There's a reason why giving difficult feedback or even loving criticism can feel like a dilemma. "It pains us to embarrass or hurt other people," Bohns says. So we don't tend to like doing it. In fact, there's a name for the phenomenon —the MUM effect, or minimizing unpleasant messages.
But with care and intention, it's possible to make informed choices about when to speak up or stay quiet, no matter how small or big the situation. Bohns shares three questions to ask yourself before sharing an opinion.
When you decide to tell someone something, remember you're sharing two things: the message itself, and the fact thatyouare choosing to speak up at all, Bohns says.
People often spend far too much time worrying about thecontentof their messages, she says. "But the choice of saying something at all communicates so much. It says, 'I see you. I care about your suffering. I want to help you in some way.'"
D'oh! I can't believe I did that! Graceful ways to handle awkward moments
So, before telling your boss/spouse/mother-in-law how youreallyfeelabout that new haircut, Bohn says to consider whether your feedback is actionable.
Honesty is only the best policy if your opinion is going to help someone "perform better or avoid embarrassment or learn something about themselves." If your feedback is mean-spirited, unrelated to the matter at hand or simply can't be enacted, you're probably better off holding your tongue.
For example, flat-out telling your roommate the cake she baked for your birthday tastes terrible? That's just mean. But if she bakes that same cake to enter into a baking competition? It would be meannotto offer her some feedback!
Before you open your mouth, reflect on your own motivations. Are you sharing your opinion to be kind — or just avoiding your own discomfort?Abi Inman/NPRhide caption
Just because you don't want to share the truth doesn't mean the person on the receiving end shouldn't or wouldn't want to hear what you have to say.
A 2022 survey, for example, found thatpeople consistently underestimate others' desire for feedback. In the study, researchers put visible smudges of lipstick, chocolate or marker on their faces. Then, without acknowledging those smudges, they went out on the street asking random people to participate in a survey on a different topic.
COMIC: Still cringing about that awkward moment? Here's what to do about it
Less than 3% of the survey participants spoke up, even though the smudges were something the researchers "clearly could have done something about and would have wanted to know," says Bohns.
So, if you choose to stay silent when your new co-worker keeps mispronouncing the name of the company CEO, for example,reflect on your own motivations. "Are you being kind, or are you avoiding your own discomfort?" writes Bohns in her book. Speaking up may help your colleague in this instance.
Has anyone ever given you advice about a topicyou knew more about than they did? Or misjudged how much you knew based on how you looked?
When in doubt, don't assume you know what information the other person wants or needs from you. Pre-assessing how valuable the truth is to someone else, or their ability to handle it, can quickly make well-meaning feedback sound patronizing, writes Bohns in her book.
So just ask the other person if they want the feedback you have to share. "Give them the autonomy, then respect their decision, whatever it might be," she says.

Good conversations take time and attention. Here's how to have better ones.Having good conversations is an art form. Former NPR host Sam Sanders tapped longtime radio host and podcaster Celeste Headlee for her tips for really listening and connecting.
4 negotiation tactics to try in everyday life. People often use negotiation tactics in business environments. But you can also use them to get your roommate to clean up, figure out where to eat for dinner or decide on which car to buy.
How to receive critical feedback.Receiving feedback doesn't necessarily have to be terrifying, according to Shanita Williams, a feedback coach, professor and author ofFeedback Mentality. In this episode, Williams and Stacy-Marie Ishmael, a writer and editor, provide five tips to make receiving feedback a little less scary.

F1 Q&A: How good is Hamilton and how long can he stay in F1? - BBC Sport
'He was in a league of his own' - Benson on Norris' Brazil GP win
McLaren's Lando Norris converted pole position into a race win at a wet-dry-wet Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday.
Max Verstappen came through the field to take second after starting at the back of the grid because of an engine penalty, while his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar was on the podium in third.
Mercedes sealed the constructors' championship for the first time since 2021 at Interlagos following a fourth-place finish for George Russell and fifth for new world champion Kimi Antonelli.
Here BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
Lewis Hamilton has just completed his 400th F1 grand prix, with more than 100 of these races having him on pole position. There are drivers with a better pole percentage than this, so just how good is he and for how much longer can he stay at the top? - Clive
Lewis Hamilton is unquestionably one of the greatest Formula 1 drivers in history.
He's statistically the most successful - with the most race wins and pole positions.
He's tied with Michael Schumacher for the most championships with seven, and many would - and do - argue he should have eight, given the controversy of themishandled final race of the 2021 season.
Greatness as an F1 driver is about more than raw statistics, but even so Hamilton has consistently proved to be at the very highest level, with a series of outstanding drives in races that will go down in history as some of the greatest ever.
Examples of those would be the 2008 British Grand Prix and the 2021 Brazilian Grand Prix, along with many others.
All of this should go without saying.
He's also won races in nearly all his seasons - the only exceptions being 2022, 2023 and 2025.
There is no question that, within the context of his remarkable career, Hamilton struggled relatively in the era of 'ground-effect' cars from 2022-25.
He was beaten by Mercedes team-mate George Russell in two of their three seasons together, and looked a shadow of his usual self against Charles Leclerc in 2025.
Those performances led some to question why a driver formerly famed and lauded for his adaptability did not seem as able to adapt to the driving style required of those cars.
And that, in turn, led to questions as to whether the fact he apparently could not was related to his age - he is now 41.
But with this year's cars, Hamilton is back in much more familiar territory, is performing extremely well again and is neck-and-neck with Leclerc.
Those questions about the four years from 2022-25 will remain just that, but there is no doubt Hamilton is sensitive to them. He has referenced them a number of times this year, including last weekend in Brazil, when the topic of his 400th race came up.
"I never ever thought that I would be reaching numbers like that," he said. "It's crazy because I still feel young, and regardless of the things that people say, you saw my pole last week, I still have the pace, I still have the speed and I still have the dedication, which is most important and the focus. For me, that number is kind of irrelevant."
Longevity in sport depends on many factors, and each athlete is different.
On the face of it, however, there is no obvious reason why, on an age front, Hamilton cannot continue for a good few more years - Fernando Alonso is 45 and is still performing at an extremely high level, as he proved yet again in Brazil at the weekend.
Hamilton has said he wants to race at least until F1 returns to Africa, which will not be until 2030 at the earliest, when he, too, will be 45.
For that, he will need at least one new contract, as his current one with Ferrari is believed to end next year.
Norris sparkles in Sao Paulo despite firework mishap
Norris brilliant in wet & Verstappen recovery extraordinary - driver ratings
We heard, and saw, a lot of 'yo-yo racing' in the first half of the season. This seems to have reduced. What has changed? - Ali
'Yo-yo racing' was a term coined at the start of this year for a new character of on-track battle in which cars swapped positions multiple times over a series of laps.
This was caused by the new power-units introduced this year, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power and are fundamentally energy starved.
The operations of these engines included 'overtake' and 'boost' modes.
'Boost' is a facility for a driver to demand extra electrical energy whenever he wants, as long as the battery has charge.
'Overtake' mode gives a driver following within one second of a car in front an extra 0.5MJ of energy recovery and deployment capability per lap.
At the start of the season, this - combined with the teams' and drivers' relative unfamiliarity with the new technology - led to a number of examples of yo-yo racing in the early grands prix.
This is where one driver has more electrical energy available, uses it to overtake, whereupon the driver behind now has more and overtakes back, and so on.
This has been less prevalent recently and there are two reasons for that.
Primarily, the tracks in recent weeks have been less 'energy-starved'. And the more energy-starved a car is at a track, the more likelihood there is for yo-yo racing.
The overtaking comes from the variation in energy levels, and being at tracks where drivers can't use all the energy they want all the time.
On top of that, drivers and teams have now been using the engines for a season and are much more on top of how to use them, and therefore how not to leave themselves vulnerable.
At the same time, rule changes have been introduced since the start of the season to reduce the impact of energy starvation, such as imposing energy limits on tracks where it is a major issue. This flattens out the peaks and troughs in energy availability.
And into next year and beyond further steps are being taken to make the engines more "normal" in operation - by changing the energy split to 60-40 in two steps by 2028.
This is almost certainly going to lead to the frequency of overtaking reducing, while the drivers become happier with how the cars feel to drive.
Whether the audience perceives that as better or worse racing remains to be seen.

How Long Can You Expect Your PC RAM To Last?
How long can you expect your PC RAM to last?
Individual RAM needs may be the biggest factor to lifespan
ByRoger FingasNov. 8, 2026 5:30 pm ESTTanit Boonruen/Getty ImagesAdd Engadget on Google:Preferred SourceGoogle Discover
We probably don't need to remind you thatRAM prices are out of control, spiraling into the sky like a broken rocket because of the unending growth of AI data centers. Companies like Apple have had toraise the cost of existing devicesto keep up profit margins, and newer products are often launching with eye-watering price tags.Valve's Steam Machinecosts over $1,000 — which is in line with a comparable gaming PC, but it was originally intended to be much cheaper, probably closer to $750. There's no telling how expensive Sony and Microsoft's next consoles will be.
This makes clinging onto the RAM you have particularly important. Replacement memory could potentially be unaffordable, never mind buying or upgrading to an entirely new computer. In fact, companies like Intel are evenbacktracking to support cheaper DDR4 RAM, despite DDR6 already being on the horizon. The good news here is that in terms of durability, your RAM will probably survive until you buy a new PC, regardless of how many years away that might be. Whether you'll tolerate the performance barriers of older modules is another matter. The demands of PC apps are always evolving, after all.
The factors impacting your RAM's lifespan
Stenko Vladislav Vitalievich/Getty Images
While it's tough to track down hard figures,PCWorldclaims that on average, the material longevity of RAM should fall anywhere between 3 and 15 years. That's obviously an extremely broad range. It's very plausible, however, when you consider the range of factors involved. For one, there's initial manufacturing quality. While it's hard to go wrong with any of the major brands out there — such as G.Skill, Samsung and Corsair — there's always the possibility of a defect, since quality control is never perfect. If you turn to an obscure brand, you're taking an even bigger gamble.
More significantly, different users put RAM under different workloads. In a PC mostly tapped for browsing, email, streaming and light gaming, there isn't much strain. But if you're handling hours of tasks like video editing, AI processing or photorealistic 3D gaming, you're naturally stretching your RAM to the limits. All of the electricity for reads and writes generates waste heat, slowly wearing down your RAM's circuitry.
Some people take their RAM to the limits and beyond by overclocking it. This boosts performance, but can push heat past intended design tolerances, at least without additional cooling. Ambient conditions play a part as well, say if your CPU and GPU are generating a lot of heat, or voltage stability is inconsistent. Lastly, there's the potential for quasi-random failures such as static shock. Your PC should always be well-grounded.
How performance gaps can force upgrades
Realistically, older DDR4 RAM is plenty fast for most people. DDR5 can deliver meaningful improvements in tasks like gaming, yet even then, CPU and GPU speeds are going to have a deeper impact. Also, quantity can matter more than quality. If you're doing a lot of multitasking, you're easily better off with 32GB of DDR4 than 16GB of DDR5. Google Chrome alone can consume over 8GB of RAM if you have a dozen or so tabs open.
It's really the link between RAM and CPU performance that's the killer. Normally, motherboards designed for the latest CPU sockets are also built with DDR5 RAM in mind, and they're not backwards compatible with DDR4, let alone DDR3. Opting for a DDR4-compatible motherboard may place serious limits on CPU speed unless you specifically hunt down one of the recent options (like Intel's) designed to circumvent the memory crisis.
The gist is that if you want to stay on the cutting edge of computing, you may be forced to upgrade the kind of RAM you're using long before what you've got expires. Even five years can be an eternity in PC evolution, never mind 10 or more. It's only the people putting their PCs through the wringer — whether in terms of prolonged workload or excessive overclocking — who should seriously be worried about sudden death.

FAA lifts nationwide ground stop that blocked takeoffs for hours
A communications problem shut down takeoffs across the US on Friday afternoon before it was lifted more than four hours later.
A view of an information board at the Chicago O’Hare International Airport, filled with waiting passengers on November 13, 2026. Photo by Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu via Getty Images)Anadolu via Getty ImagesRichard Lawler
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.
Takeoffs from airports throughout the US largely stopped on Friday after the FAA issued a national ground stop at 3:44PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” while planes in the air will be allowed to land. The FAAtweeted just after 5PM ETthat, “There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.”
More than four hours after the stop was issued, officials announced it was lifted at 8:15PM ET and that flights will resume.
In a press conference announcing that the stop had been lifted, Transportation Secretary Ryan Duffy blamed an aging air traffic control system that he is pursuing funds to replace, saying that the TRACONs (Terminal Radar Approach Control) in the air traffic control centers “started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and the communications from airplanes.” He said that the devices that had the issue were analog telecom devices, where the switches / routers “got overloaded with data” and started to show inconsistency.
It’s unclear how many flights will be able to take off and when, as they now face problems of overloaded aircraft and flight crews that have run out of time to operate the planes, meaning many people will be stuck where they are for the time being and more flights will be delayed or canceled.
The flight tracking siteFlightAwarelists 9,124 US flights as delayed and 5,901 flights canceled as of 8:39PM ET.
According to CNN, the last nationwide ground stop in 2023 lasted for about 90 minutesafter the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system for pilots went down, and the last one prior to that was after the attacks on September 11th, 2001.
Speaking to reporters at the White House on Friday afternoon, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters that there is currently no reason to suspect a cyberattack or other national security threat, or any connection to the recentMicrosoft Outlook outage, but that so far no cause has been ruled out for the “telecommunications outage.”
When asked about any possible connection to the cloud-based AI Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories(SMART) systemthat was activatednationwideon November 10th, he said they were looking into that. Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company that designed the system and was awarded a12-year $875 million contractin June to deploy it, denied any connection,tweeting“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”
Jon Ostrower ofThe Air Currentreports that the outage began with the Chicago air traffic control center, followed by centers in Boston, Washington, New York, and Minneapolis, and as the FAA issued a ground stop for aircraft flying east, more facilities began reporting problems. He says the problems are disrupting both the radar and radio frequencies used by air traffic controllers and pilots, while a CNN update on Friday cited an unnamed source claiming the FAA “doesn’t know yet what is going on,” with no clear answers about the cause.
Updated, Friday, November 13th:Added that the stop has been lifted.

FAA lifts ground stop after four hours, but flight cancellations will stretch into the weekendSkip Navigation
MarketsBusinessInvestingTechPolitics & PolicyVideoWatchlistInvesting ClubPROLivestreamMenu
The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, disrupting thousands of departing of flights.
The agency reported communication problems affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers.
Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare, and the last was in January 2023 after a failure of a pilot communication system.
Follow your favorite stocksCREATE FREE ACCOUNTPassengers queue at the Southwest Airlines desk to speak with a representative at Eppley Airfield in Omaha, Neb., on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026.Nikos Frazier | Omaha World-Herald | Lee Newspapers | Getty Images
The Federal Aviation Administration halted flight departures across the country for more than four hours on Friday, the second time it had issued a nationwide ground stop since 9/11, blaming communications failures that affected multiple air traffic control centers. More than 10,000 flights were disrupted, with delays and cancellations set to stretch into the weekend.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed aging air traffic control infrastructure for the problem.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday at the White House that there was no indication that the issues were a threat to the United States. He later said at a press conference that it doesn't appear to be a cyber attack, and that it "appears this was mechanically driven."
The FAA canceled the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday.
The agency earlier said in post on X that there was a "temporary telecommunications outage" and that it halted flights out of an "abundance of caution."
While the FAA lifted the ground stop, travel chaos continued at airports, which were forced to find places for parked planes. Delays were set to continue.
Travelers wait inside San Francisco International Airport in San Francisco, California on Nov. 13, 2026.Jeniece Pettitt | CNBC
Carriers were preparing to cancel flights as the disruption wore on.JetBlue Airwaystold staff it would cancel the remainder of the day's flights, aside from European routes, as well as others scheduled for Saturday so that crews and planes are in place to resume operations, according to a memo seen by CNBC.
A ground stop halts flights at their departure point. Disruptions tend to snowball if ground stops drag on as flight crews reach their maximum number of duty hours for a day.
There were 11,000 flights scheduled to depart U.S. airports after 4 p.m. ET on Friday, according to flight-data firm Cirium. There were about 600 diverted flights on Friday, 104 of them sent to other airports, Cirium said.
Travelers wait inside JFK International Airport in New York on Nov. 13, 2026.Gabriela Riccardi for CNBC
International flights had started taking off from coastal hubs before 6 p.m. ET.
Flights will be allowed to depart as en route traffic facilities recover, "through coordination with the air traffic control system," the FAA said earlier.
When it issued the ground stop at about 4 p.m., the FAA said the communications issues were "impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers." These facilities guide airplanes at high altitudes along their routes.
The FAA's technicians are investigating, the agency said.
Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare.
In January 2023, the FAAhalted flightsbecause of issues with a pilot alert system. Before that, traffic was halted nationwide after the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.
watch nowVIDEO15:5715:57Why the U.S. doesn't have enough air traffic controllersAirlines
Technical issues have repeatedly snarled air traffic in the U.S. in recent years.
In September,hundreds of flightsinto Newark, New Jersey, and Philadelphia were canceled, delayed or diverted after aVerizonfiber cable was accidentally cut. Officials said it occurred during construction in New Jersey, severing a backup feed of key data for air traffic controllers.
In 2025, air traffic controllers lost contact with aircraft heading to and fromNewark Liberty International Airport, anequipment failurethat led to massive flight delays and raised more concerns aboutaging U.S. aviation infrastructureand staffing shortages.
"It's going to continue to fail," Duffy said of U.S. air traffic control infrastructure. The U.S. is in the middle of anoverhaulof the technology, and Duffy urged lawmakers for more funding on Friday.
Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis, the FAA said.
The major U.S. airlines issued statements saying they would work with customers who were affected by the ground stop and encouraged travelers to check for updates.

FAA orders third nationwide ground stop in its history - Ars TechnicaSkip to content
Text settingsStory textSizeSmallStandardLargeWidth*StandardWideLinksStandardOrange* Subscribers only
On Friday afternoon, days after expanding use of anAI tool, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, halting departures from all US airports. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy announced the ground stopon X, citing a “communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” Duffy promised updates as more information is known and said FAA staff were troubleshooting the problem.
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the ground stop was not prompted by a security threat. “This is a telecommunications outage out of the FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all of the flights,” Mullinsaid. “There’s no indication as of yet that this is a nefarious attack against us.”
Mullin said the FAA would handle incoming international flights on a case-by-case basis.
This is only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. The first, and most memorable, came during the attacks of September 11, 2001, when the FAA stopped all civilian departures nationwide and subsequently ordered all airborne aircraft to land. Commercial flights did not take off again until September 13.Flights were also groundedfor less than two hours the morning of January 11, 2023, after itsNotice to Air Missionssystem suffered an outage.
Unfortunately for travelers, based on what is known so far, this is likely to be a lengthy ground stop. fact_units.text: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop that blocked takeoffs for hours | The VergeSkip to main contentThe homepage
FAA lifts nationwide ground stop that blocked takeoffs for hours
A communications problem shut down takeoffs across the US on Friday afternoon before it was lifted more than four hours later.
A view of an information board at the Chicago O’Hare International Airport, filled with waiting passengers on November 13, 2026.
Photo by Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu via Getty Images)Anadolu via Getty ImagesRichard Lawler
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment.
He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Takeoffs from airports throughout the US largely stopped on Friday after the FAA issued a national ground stop at 3:44PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” while planes in the air will be allowed to land.
The FAAtweeted just after 5PM ETthat, “There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted.
Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.”
More than four hours after the stop was issued, officials announced it was lifted at 8:15PM ET and that flights will resume.

In a press conference announcing that the stop had been lifted, Transportation Secretary Ryan Duffy blamed an aging air traffic control system that he is pursuing funds to replace, saying that the TRACONs (Terminal Radar Approach Control) in the air traffic control centers “started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and the communications from airplanes.” He said that the devices that had the issue were analog telecom devices, where the switches / routers “got overloaded with data” and started to show inconsistency.

It’s unclear how many flights will be able to take off and when, as they now face problems of overloaded aircraft and flight crews that have run out of time to operate the planes, meaning many people will be stuck where they are for the time being and more flights will be delayed or canceled.
The flight tracking siteFlightAwarelists 9,124 US flights as delayed and 5,901 flights canceled as of 8:39PM ET.

According to CNN, the last nationwide ground stop in 2023 lasted for about 90 minutesafter the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system for pilots went down, and the last one prior to that was after the attacks on September 11th, 2001.

Speaking to reporters at the White House on Friday afternoon, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters that there is currently no reason to suspect a cyberattack or other national security threat, or any connection to the recentMicrosoft Outlook outage, but that so far no cause has been ruled out for the “telecommunications outage.”

When asked about any possible connection to the cloud-based AI Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories(SMART) systemthat was activatednationwideon November 10th, he said they were looking into that.

Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company that designed the system and was awarded a12-year $875 million contractin June to deploy it, denied any connection,tweeting“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”

Jon Ostrower ofThe Air Currentreports that the outage began with the Chicago air traffic control center, followed by centers in Boston, Washington, New York, and Minneapolis, and as the FAA issued a ground stop for aircraft flying east, more facilities began reporting problems.

He says the problems are disrupting both the radar and radio frequencies used by air traffic controllers and pilots, while a CNN update on Friday cited an unnamed source claiming the FAA “doesn’t know yet what is going on,” with no clear answers about the cause.
Updated, Friday, November 13th:Added that the stop has been lifted.

FAA lifts ground stop after four hours, but flight cancellations will stretch into the weekendSkip Navigation
The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, disrupting thousands of departing of flights.
The agency reported communication problems affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers.
Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare, and the last was in January 2023 after a failure of a pilot communication system.
Follow your favorite stocksCREATE FREE ACCOUNTPassengers queue at the Southwest Airlines desk to speak with a representative at Eppley Airfield in Omaha, Neb., on Friday, Nov.
13, 2026.Nikos Frazier | Omaha World-Herald | Lee Newspapers | Getty Images

The Federal Aviation Administration halted flight departures across the country for more than four hours on Friday, the second time it had issued a nationwide ground stop since 9/11, blaming communications failures that affected multiple air traffic control centers.
More than 10,000 flights were disrupted, with delays and cancellations set to stretch into the weekend.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed aging air traffic control infrastructure for the problem.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday at the White House that there was no indication that the issues were a threat to the United States.
He later said at a press conference that it doesn't appear to be a cyber attack, and that it "appears this was mechanically driven."
The FAA canceled the ground stop at 8:15 p.m.
The agency earlier said in post on X that there was a "temporary telecommunications outage" and that it halted flights out of an "abundance of caution."
While the FAA lifted the ground stop, travel chaos continued at airports, which were forced to find places for parked planes.

GOP state officials appeal block on 2028 mail voting limitsSome Republican state officials are reviving a bid for mail-in voting restrictions for the 2028 election by appealing a court order blocking the Postal Service from carrying out a revised ballot rule.
GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election
An election worker sorts mail-in ballots at the Miami-Dade County Supervisor of Elections Office in Doral for Florida's primary election in August.Lynne Sladky/APhide caption
Voting for this year's midterm elections just concluded, but Republican officials in a number of states are already looking to shape how votes are cast in 2028.
Twelve GOP state attorneys general are pushing to revive the president's bid for mail-in voting restrictions in time for the 2028 election.
On Thursday, theystarted the processof appealinga September orderby U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, one of the two judges who blocked the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a plan released in response to anexecutive order by President Trump.
The Republican state attorneys general represent Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas. It's not clear, however, how long some of these states will continue this case, given that Democrats won up and down the ballot in the midterms. In Texas and Kansas, Democratic candidates are set to take control of their states' attorney general's offices in January.
The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue
In September, the Supreme Courtrefused to pausea similar ruling by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, who is based in Boston. That order stopped USPS from working on its revised rule for federal ballot mail, but it only applied to this year's midterm elections.
Nichols' preliminary injunction blocks USPS from implementing the plan for all federal elections, including the 2028 race.
It's not clear if the Trump administration plans to appeal Nichols' ruling by Friday's deadline for filing a court notice. Asked about the Justice Department's plans, DOJ spokesperson Matthew Tragesser replied in an email that the department doesn't comment on ongoing litigation.
The blocked rule — which the Postal Service released in late August — would require states to turn over lists of voters' names and addresses in order to have them delivered by USPS.
Tens of millions cast ballots for midterms despite worries of Trump's interference
Nichols, a Washington, D.C.-based judge who was nominated by Trump, found that the mailing agency likely has no power to impose that requirement on states.
"As the Government concedes, the Postal Service could issue (and enforce) the Rule only if Congress gave it the authority to do so, but here no statute grants the Postal Service the power to issue key parts of the Rule," Nichols wrote.
The administration's earlier push to put these new restrictions in place for the midterms alarmed many election officials, who were concerned about last-minute changes causing major disruptions to the tens of millions who regularly vote by mail. Some voters with disabilities and those in places without polling sites, they feared, could have lost the ability to exercise their right to cast a ballot.
Awhistleblower reportclaimed the online system officials would need to use to follow USPS' revised ballot requirements had not been properly tested and could have resulted in many eligible voters not getting their mail-in ballots in time or at all.
While the Supreme Court ultimately stopped implementation of the USPS rule for the midterms, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented from that ruling.
Fellow conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh said in a concurring opinion that he believed state and local election officials did not have enough time to "reasonably implement the rule" this time. But Kavanaugh noted that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority."

Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say | TechCrunch
Image Credits:Heather Diehl / Getty ImagesVenture
Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
Marina TemkinDominic-Madori Davis2:43 PM PST · November 13, 2026
It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’sembattled CEOwho co-founded and led the company for 33 years,had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.
Over the last several years, Nvidia has been aprolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.
Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.
“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.
Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.
Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress,is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux ofthe billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.
“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”
Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.
For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It boughtHugging Face this year for $13 billion(expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to theWall Street Journal.
“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”
It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.
If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Googleannounced two new chipsthis week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)
Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.
Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.
While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.
Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.
Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.
“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.
Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

Bloomberg Details Web Of Chinese AI Companies With Smuggled NVIDIA Chips Linked To Alice Huang
Bloomberg details web of Chinese AI companies with smuggled NVIDIA chips linked to Alice Huang
The NVIDIA chips involved are banned in China.
ByMariella MoonNov. 13, 2026 7:58 am ESTSean Gallup/Getty ImagesAdd Engadget on Google:Preferred SourceGoogle Discover
A Chinese company with ties to Alice Huang procured NVIDIA AI chips banned in the country, which were then installed at a Shanghai AI facility that also has ties to Alice Huang, according toBloomberg. The publication says the documents it has reviewed for its report shows explicit evidence that there's a network of Chinese companies, which have managed to get their hands on NVIDIA chips that weren't supposed to be sold in China, with Huang at the center.
US officials believe that Alice Huang is a spyrecruited by China's main intelligence agencyto target NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. The goal was apparently to learn more about America's AI plans and to get Jensen Huang to persuade the US government to let his company ship its more advanced chips to China. Before hestepped down as CEO of NVIDIA, Jensen Huang reportedlyadmittedin a staff memo that he had an affair with Alice Huang.
To the public, Alice was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, but the reports that had come out since the issue blew up paint a different picture of who she truly was.Bloombergsays the NVIDIA chips listed in the documents it reviewed were sold to Aperia Cloud Services, an NVIDIA Cloud Partner in Singapore. Aperia purchased 22 servers from Dell containing NVIDIA H800 chips, which are banned in China. According to the report, Dell cut off business ties with Aperia in February 2025 due to concerns around the deal.
Bloombergfound the hardware details in filings from a company called Shanghai Longteng Intelligent Computing, which was set up by Alice a decade ago. They were documented as part of the information the company had to submit to the Chinese government, since it was using its servers as a collateral for financing. While Alice hasn't been part of Shanghai Longteng since 2017 — and the documents didn't say if she was personally involved in the procurement of the chips — Huang Yu, who was identified as her sister, was the one who took over as majority owner. The filings also revealed that the company's servers included 52 units made by Super Micro Computer Inc. Those units were equipped with NVIDIA's H100 orH200chips, which can't be sold to Chinese companies without express permission from the US government.
The Shanghai AI facility where the smuggled NVIDIA units were installed is called the Yangtze River Delta Project, whichBloombergsays also has ties to Alice Huang. Its president is Kang Wei, who is being reported as Alice's husband and the personwho introduced her to Jensen Huang. Alice's company Megaspeed also presented a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project to its investors in 2024 and claimed that it was its largest AI facility. Former NVIDIA-CEO Jensen Huang isdue to testify before Congress this month, and it's likely all of this information will be pored over by officials in the run-up to the event.

article.title: Hệ thống xổ số NBA mới gây bất lợi cho Memphis Grizzlies trong năm 2027
article.summary: Thay đổi trong quy định xổ số NBA đang khiến Memphis Grizzlies đối mặt với rủi ro lớn khi quyền chọn cầu thủ từ Utah Jazz bị hạn chế, bất chấp phong độ sa sút của đối thủ.
body: Hệ thống xổ số NBA vừa được cải tổ đang tạo ra những tác động không mong muốn đối với Memphis Grizzlies, đặc biệt trong việc khai thác quyền chọn cầu thủ từ Utah Jazz tại kỳ NBA Draft 2027. Dù Utah Jazz đang trải qua khởi đầu mùa giải đầy khó khăn với thành tích 1-11, Memphis Grizzlies không còn khả năng tận dụng tối đa sự sa sút này để giành lấy vị trí chọn cầu thủ cao nhất như dưới thể thức cũ.

Theo quy định mới, các đội bóng không được phép sở hữu quyền chọn trong top 5 trong ba năm liên tiếp. Do Utah Jazz đã có các lượt chọn trong top 5 ở cả hai kỳ Draft 2025 và 2026, lượt chọn mà Memphis Grizzlies sở hữu thông qua thương vụ Jaren Jackson Jr. sẽ bị hạn chế, không thể rơi vào nhóm 5 vị trí dẫn đầu. Điều này đồng nghĩa với việc vị trí cao nhất mà Grizzlies có thể đạt được là lượt chọn thứ 6.

Memphis Grizzlies là đội bóng duy nhất bỏ phiếu chống lại hệ thống xổ số mới này vì lo ngại những hạn chế về thứ hạng. Trong bối cảnh kỳ Draft 2027 được đánh giá là kém chất lượng hơn so với hai năm trước, việc bị chặn ở vị trí thứ 6 thay vì có cơ hội cạnh tranh các vị trí đầu bảng được xem là một tổn thất đáng kể cho kế hoạch xây dựng đội hình của Grizzlies. Sự thay đổi này làm thay đổi hoàn toàn giá trị của tài sản mà Memphis đã dày công tích lũy thông qua các giao dịch chuyển nhượng trước đó.

article.title: Tổng thống Ukraine hoan nghênh nỗ lực của Mỹ đưa châu Âu vào đàm phán hòa bình
article.summary: Tổng thống Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky hoan nghênh cam kết từ các đặc phái viên Mỹ về việc đưa đại diện Liên minh Châu Âu tham gia vòng đàm phán hòa bình tiếp theo với Nga.
body: Tổng thống Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky đã chính thức lên tiếng hoan nghênh cam kết từ các đặc phái viên Mỹ. Theo đó, đại diện Liên minh Châu Âu sẽ được bao gồm trong vòng đàm phán hòa bình tiếp theo với Nga sau thời gian dài đứng ngoài các tiến xúc tiến ngoại giao.

Động thái này diễn ra trong bối cảnh các đặc phái viên Mỹ gồm Jared Kushner và Steve Witkoff đã có cuộc gặp với ông Zelensky tại Dublin vào tối thứ Năm. Chuyến công tác này nằm trong chuỗi hoạt động ngoại giao con thoi, nối tiếp cuộc gặp trực tiếp với Tổng thống Nga Vladimir Putin tại Moscow trước đó cùng ngày.

Trước đó, các nhà lãnh đạo châu Âu bày tỏ nhiều quan ngại sâu sắc về an ninh khu vực khi chiến sự kéo dài. Việc đưa đại diện châu Âu vào bàn đàm phán được kỳ vọng sẽ đảm bảo khối này có tiếng nói quyết định trong các vấn đề liên quan trực tiếp đến tương lai an ninh lục địa.

Dù vậy, lập trường của điện Kremlin về vấn đề này vẫn chưa có sự nhượng bộ rõ ràng. Trong cuộc gặp tại Moscow, phía Nga khẳng định các yêu cầu về lãnh thổ và điều kiện chấm dứt xung đột không thay đổi, đồng thời cuộc gặp trước đó tại Abu Dhabi cũng chưa đạt được bước đột phá.

Bên cạnh tiến trình ngoại giao, các bên cũng ghi nhận một số diễn biến nhân đạo đáng chú ý khi Nga và Ukraine đạt thỏa thuận thực hiện một đợt trao đổi tù nhân lớn. Phía Mỹ kỳ vọng thỏa thuận này sẽ sớm đưa hàng nghìn người trở về đoàn tụ với gia đình.

Somehow, some way, Victor Wembanyama seems to have leveled up.

Matching Tim Duncan in 30-point, 5-block Spurs games
If you needed a reminder, Wembanyama is just 22 years old. He won't turn 23 until Jan. 4, 2027. Yet, after officially "arriving" last season by leading the Spurs to the NBA Finals, he's already setting some all-time team records for a franchise that has had a few elite big men.

Why NBA Draft Lottery system could cost Grizzlies more than any team in 2027 as Jazz struggle | Sporting NewsSkip to main content
Why NBA Draft Lottery system could cost Grizzlies more than any team in 2027 as Jazz struggle
TheGrizzliesare undoubtedly encouraged by the play of some of their young players early this season, but they could still be in line for the No. 1 pick — under the NBA's former draft lottery system.
After the system was overhauled earlier this year, Memphis stands to miss out on what could've been a franchise-changing result.
The Grizzlies own an additional first-round pick in 2027, and the brutal 1-11 start by theJazzwould have made their pick likely to go to Memphis under the previous format. Now, however, the Grizzlies won't able to take full advantage of Utah's struggles.
Grizzlies basketball now lives on DAZN
Catch every local Grizzlies broadcast, exclusively on DAZN
Why NBA Draft Lottery system could hurt Grizzlies
The Grizzlies own the most favorable first-round pick among the Jazz,CavaliersandTimberwolvesin 2027. While Cleveland has struggled out of the gate, relative to expectations, neither team has been anywhere close to as bad as 1-11 Utah.
If this were the 2025-26 season, the Jazz would be in firm contention for the No. 1 pick. Under the new system, the worst three teams have worse odds than the teams behind them, but the number of truly bad teams this season means Utah could very well wind up in the sweet spot with the highest odds.
The Grizzlies, in turn, would be in firm contention for the top pick despite a strong start to the season. Under the new format, that isn't the case.
Teams cannot land top-five picks in three consecutive years, and the Jazz already had top-five picks in both 2025 and 2026. Even though the pick would go to the Grizzlies as part of the Jaren Jackson Jr. trade, it still cannot land inside the top five in 2027.
It is worth noting that the Jazz cannot receive top-5 pick in the 2027 NBA Draft under the new rules and format since they've been in the top 5 each of the previous two drafts. However, Memphis owns this pick, so that restriction would impact the Grizzlies.
— Brett Siegel (@BrettSiegelNBA)November 11, 2026
The Grizzlies were the only team to vote against the new lottery system for this very reason: the highest they can land if they get Utah's 2027 pick is No. 6. In a draft considered to be weaker than the last two, that's much different than being No. 1 or No. 2.

Afghanistan Premier League: Female players express disappointment at overseas players' involvement - BBC Sport
Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,
Firooza Amiri and Nahida Sapan were among the Afghan women's players to flee to Australia
ByFfion Wynne,BBC Sport JournalistandAlison Mitchell,BBC Stumped host
Afghan women's cricketers have accused overseas players signing up for the inaugural Afghanistan Premier League of sending a message to the world that women suffering in the country "can simply be ignored".
Women's participation in sport has been effectively outlawed since the Taliban's return to power in 2021, and many of Afghanistan's female cricketersleft the country for their own safety.
The men'sfranchise league is expected to start in December in the UAE, though it is yet to be sanctioned by the International Cricket Council (ICC).
In September, the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) urged players toreconsider their involvementand batterOllie Pope withdrew.
"For five years, girls in Afghanistan have been denied the right to play cricket and many other basic rights," Nahida Sapan, who captained the Afghanistan Refugee Women's XI on this summer's tour of England, told theBBC Stumped podcast.
"Foreign players had a real opportunity to stand with millions of Afghan women and girls by choosing not to participate.
"It may have seemed like a small action, but it could have sent a powerful message and put pressure on those responsible.
"This is not about being against cricket or Afghan men's cricket. It is about standing up for basic human rights."
Eight English players were signed in the draft on Tuesday, alongside players from Scotland, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand.
England's Alex Hales, Tymal Mills, Joe Clarke, Olly Stone, Moeen Ali, Luke Wood, Tom Moores and Chris Wood were all signed. Scotland's George Munsey also secured a deal, as did Ireland all-rounder Curtis Campher.
Other England players including Dawid Malan and James Vince also put their names into the draft.
England will have more overseas representation than any other country in the Afghan league.
The major names signed from other nations include Sri Lanka internationals Kusal Perera, Wanindu Hasaranga, Dushmantha Chameera and Kamindu Mendis, Australian batter D'Arcy Short, South Africa spinner Imran Tahir and Bangladesh all-rounder Shakib Al Hasan.
The ECB has refused to schedule bilateral cricket with Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power - a stance Australia also adopts.
England have, however, continued to play against Afghanistan at global events, including World Cups in both limited-overs formats and the Champions Trophy, which resulted in calls from MPs for their game in 2025to be boycotted.
"For me, the women and girls of Afghanistan come first," said Sapan. "Their rights, dignity and freedom matter more than any league or sporting opportunity.
"Taking part in this league without acknowledging what is happening to Afghan women risks sending the message to the world that their suffering can simply be ignored."
Afghan women ask ICC for 'clear answers' on future
Afghan women tell the BBC their lives are unrecognisable after five years of Taliban rule
Afghanistan's women's players have repeatedly called on the ICC to recognise them once again as an international team, and commit to long-term funding.
Without official ICC recognition, they play as the Afghan Refugee Women's Team.
In April 2025, the ICC - together with the cricket boards of England, Australia and India - announced a joint programme to provide financial support for the players, and that fundingwas extended in July.
"To every international player considering participating in this league, I believe there is a responsibility to ask difficult questions," said batter Firooza Amiri.
"You have the freedom to choose where you play, which organisations you represent and which competitions you participate in, but that freedom also comes with a responsibility to understand the systems you may be helping to support.
"I am not asking international players to turn their backs on the people of Afghanistan. I am asking them to recognise the difference between supporting Afghan people and legitimising a system that has systematically taken away women's rights."
Afghanistan men's team has retained full ICC membership despite the country's inability to meet the membership requirement of supporting a women's national side.
Amiri said their stance was not about withdrawing support for the Afghanistan men's team.
"Imagine your daughter, your sister or your wife being told that she cannot attend school simply because she is a woman," she said. "Imagine being told that she cannot play sport, pursue her ambitions or participate in public life.
"We cannot celebrate the development of cricket in Afghanistan while ignoring the complete exclusion of half of its population from the game.
"The question is whether the international cricket community is prepared to stand by its own values when it comes to Afghan women."

Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks - BBC News
Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,
US envoys Jared Kushner (left) and Steve Witkoff (right) met Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening
Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.
European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.
Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.
The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.
But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given.
US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow
Europe's security 'fundamentally reshaped' by war in Ukraine
Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."
He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table".
"He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.
Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".
Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.
Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war.
"Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.
Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common.
Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.
Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists infacilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

Putin takes hard line in US talks as Ukraine says Starlink disrupted again
Russian president says he would target any foreign troops sent to Ukraine and refuses to soften territorial demands
Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops deployed to Ukraine, in a series of hardline remarks that came as the Ukrainian military faced renewed disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service.
During the talks at the Kremlin with the US envoysJared Kushnerand Steve Witkoff on Thursday, the Russian president refused to soften his territorial demands, insisting on full control over four Ukrainian regions that Moscow claims to have annexed.
He also ruled out accepting the deployment of foreign peacekeeping troops inUkraine, describing such a move as a “continuation of war”.
Putin’s comments appeared to severely dampen hopes that a peace deal could be within reach, afterVolodymyr Zelenskyysaid there was a “window of opportunity” to reach an agreement before the end of 2026.
The latest trip to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, who have made numerous visits to Russia, was partly aimed at securing European participation in future negotiations, according to two people familiar with the talks.
Trump could be about to sell out Ukraine. Europe must get its act together, fast | Paul TaylorRead more
Speaking after the meeting, Witkoff confirmed that European representatives would join the next round of talks. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he told reporters as he boarded a plane leaving Moscow.
The US envoys will now travel to Dublin, Ireland, where they will meet Zelenskyy and debrief him on the Moscow meeting.
Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, said national security adviser Jonathan Powell would join the talks in Berlin.
Amid a flurry of diplomatic activity, including the recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the Kremlin appears to have succeeded in reframing negotiations over the war in Ukraine as part of a broader discussion about European security.
But Europe is wary of Russian attempts to focus discussions on a European security architecture, while Moscow continues to pound Ukraine with bombs and missiles.
The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told reporters: “We already have a European security architecture in place.” Kallas pointed to the cold war-era Helsinki accords andthe Budapest memorandum, which guaranteed the territorial integrity of Ukraine. “The problem is that Russia is not keeping to those agreements, so right now the focus should be that Russia actually keeps to their obligations … and they don’t attack another country again.” Focusing on a European security architecture was a “distraction” without a ceasefire, she added.
Both Washington and Moscow have been urging European leaders to appoint a single representative to lead negotiations on their behalf.
“Once a representative is appointed, a chief negotiator authorised to speak on Europe’s behalf, there will be a four-way dialogue,” Putin said on Thursday.
EU leaders are due to discuss the issue of who speaks for Europe on Friday, but so far have declined to nominate one person to speak for the bloc. One EU official said the EU would be represented by its institutions when issues concerning the union were on the table, but played down any imminent appointment. They said: “Do I expect an agreement on a special representative? My answer is no, I don’t.”
Kallas suggested she – as the EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy – should represent the EU in talks, alongside António Costa, the president of the European Council.
More than 45 European leaders are meeting in Dublin for the European Political Community summit, a gathering that brings together nearly every country on the continent, apart from the leaders of Belarus and Russia.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, played down the importance of having a single European negotiator, saying “the content determines the format”. “There is no more US support. So there [are] some mediations, fine,” he said, referring to the process led by Kushner and Witkoff. “But at the end of the day we will be the one to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”
The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said it was first necessary to get Putin to the negotiating table before deciding on a European envoy. Merz said: “It’s not about individuals. What matters is that Putin is prepared to hold talks.”
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy accused Musk’s Starlink satellite service of damaging Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian drone attacks, after Ukrainian military officials reported new restrictions on the system.
According to Zelenskyy, Starshield, a military version of Starlink funded by the Pentagon, has for several days been subject to speed limits of 100mph (161km/h) along the frontline and in Russian-occupied territory.
Similar restrictions last month prompted confusion over who had ordered them, with Musk and the Trump administration pointing fingers at each other before the service was partly restored.
The latest restrictions had made it harder for Ukrainian forces to intercept Russia’s increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy said, accusing the service of “helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine”.
Kyiv has contacted Washington to seek an explanation for the disruption, which Zelenskyy said appeared to be deliberate rather than a technical fault.

In Moscow, Witkoff and Kushner Ask Putin to Include Europe in Peace Talks - The New York Times
President Trump’s envoys went to Moscow on Thursday to seek agreement from President Vladimir V. Putin to bring Europe into talks on the war in Ukraine, as the Kremlin pushes to widen the negotiations to overhaul European security arrangements.
The envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, arrived in Russia one day after mediating peace talks in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian representatives, who spoke directly for the first time in nine months. After meeting with Mr. Putin in the Kremlin, theytraveled to Dublin to meet with and debrief President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine.
Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner are pressing to involve Europe in the talks as Russia makes clear that it will not consider a cease-fire until its broader demands to redraw Europe’s security architecture are addressed.
“We cannot conclude this deal without Europeans being at the table,” Mr. Kushner told reporters on Thursday night, speaking at the air base where he and Mr. Witkoff has just met with Mr. Zelensky, as planes for both delegations waited nearby.
Mr. Zelensky, standing next to him, said that Europewill jointhe next round of talks.
“It’s important for us, because the war is in Europe,” he said.
The Trump administration, seeking a foreign policy win after Republicans’ drubbing in the midterm elections, is making another push for peace even as Russia gives no indication that it will stop the war anytime soon, and in fact appears to be hardening some positions.
Russia has intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities ahead of a winter bombing campaign, taking advantage of Ukraine’s lack of air defenses. On Thursday, Mr. Zelensky said that Ukraine’s armed forces again faced restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the satellite internet network Starlink, and had asked U.S. officials for information.
ImageA man being rescued after his apartment was struck in Kharkiv, Ukraine, last month.Credit...Mauricio Lima for The New York Times
For Europe, getting involved in direct negotiations would be a departure from its long-held position that Russia must stop fighting first. But European officials also insist on a seat at the table if talks expand to include questions of Europe’s security.
Russia has yet to confirm that Europe will join the next set of negotiations, though Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Thursday that they are “making every effort to join the negotiations.”
At the Kremlin, Mr. Putin told Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner that he was eager to hear their assessments from “a European perspective” after their meetings with European officials in recent weeks, including in Abu Dhabi.
Mr. Putin has vented at European nations as they have replaced the United States as Ukraine’s biggest backer, asserting that it is Europe, not Russia, that wants war. On Thursday, Mr. Putin signaled to the American envoys that he was not ready for an easy compromise and that if Russia spoke with Europe’s representatives, negotiations would be tough.
“We would very much like you, distinguished gentlemen, and the American administration as a whole, to work with your European allies so that they finally make up their minds on the question of what they want: peace or war in Ukraine,” Mr. Putin said.
The Americans struck more hopeful notes. Mr. Kushner said the American side had seen “a big change with the Europeans” and “there is strong momentum and desire to engage together.”
On Thursday, President Alexander Stubb of Finlandsaid“there is a real possibility that the Europeans will be around the table, and I think that would be progress in and of itself.” Last month, Mr. Putin helda call with Mr. Stubb and his Norwegian counterpartthat some other European leaders denounced as endangering unity on Russia.
European Union leaders plan to debate who should speak on their behalf during negotiations at a lunch in Dublin on Friday — and they widely agreed on Thursday that a European presence was critical.
“Europe’s security cannot be discussed without a European voice at the table,” said Antonio Costa, president of the E.U. political leadership arm. He added that when it comes to Europe’s security architecture, “there is no need to reinvent the wheel,” stressing the importance of features like inviolable frontiers and peaceful settlement of disputes.
If Europe joins the talks, said Tatiana Stanovaya, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, it could be interpreted by Mr. Putin as a sign that his tactic of waiting out the Europeans for concessions is working.
On Wednesday, speaking at a security conference in Moscow, Aleksei Drobinin, a senior Russian diplomat, outlined proposals that he said could satisfy Moscow’s security demands regarding Europe.
Mr. Drobinin said Russia could sign bilateral agreements with European states that, “in substance, meet the criteria of mutual nonaggression pacts,” or reach “political agreements on mutually refraining from supporting each other’s adversaries in the event of aggression.” He compared these potential accords to agreements Russia has signed with Belarus, Iran and North Korea.
The Americans are seeking a sweeping agreement that would bundle questions of a cease-fire, security and territory. Speaking at the Kremlin, Mr. Putin dismissed Ukrainian assertions that he was being fed inflated claims about how much territory Russian troops controlled in Ukraine.
Mr. Putin offered to conduct a humanitarian mission in Kostiantynivka, a Ukrainian city contested by Russia and Ukraine. The effort would be similar to the recent cease-fire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. Brokered by the U.S. first lady, Melania Trump, that mission wasthe longest localized cease-fire since 2022 and helped evacuate hundredsof civilians.
Mr. Putin said such a mission would prove a point on Russia’s territorial gains. “At the same time,” he said, “we will see who controls that settlement.”
Ivan Nechepurenko covers Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, the countries of the Caucasus and Central Asia. He divides his reporting time between Moscow and Tbilisi, Georgia.
Jeanna Smialek is the Brussels bureau chief for The Times.

fact_units.text: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks - BBC News
US envoys Jared Kushner (left) and Steve Witkoff (right) met Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening
Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.
European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.

Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.
The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.
But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given.
US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow
Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."
He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table".
"He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".
Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.

Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war.

"Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.
Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common.
Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.

Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists infacilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

ByJane WitherspoonPublished on12 November 2026 - 18:30 GMT+1ShareCommentsAdd Euronews on GoogleShareFacebookTwitterFlipboardSendRedditLinkedinMessengerTelegramVKBlueskyThreadsWhatsappCopy/paste the article video embed link below:Copied
Thailand is a “geopolitically safe zone” “in a world where we see the rules based international order breaking down,” Thailand’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister tells Euronews in a wide-ranging interview in Bangkok.
Thailand’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told Euronews that as “we live in a world where we see the rules-based international order breaking down,” “we need to restore multilateralism, because nobody can go it alone.”
In a wide-ranging interview for Euronews’ newWorld Conversationglobal programme, the veteran top Thai diplomat, with over 40 years of foreign ministry service, outlined how Thailand has managed to secure a balanced approach with the United States and China at a time when the “the main global contestation is between the two superpowers whom both are friends of Thailand.”
“We ask our friends not to force us to take sides,” Sihasak explained, adding that “not taking sides does not mean being neutral as sometimes neutrality does not serve your interest.” He pointed to growing Chinese investment in electric vehicles and the US role in regional security.
A market of 700 million people, Thailand is “a geopolitically safe zone,” the deputy prime minister said in Bangkok, and therefore its strategic objective is to maintain peace and stability. In this context, he emphasized the crucial role played by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) alliance for pan-Asian stability, adding that Thailand was ready to rebuild ties with Cambodia and defended a gradual return to regional talks with Myanmar.

Malaysia’s king has warned that any attempt to challenge his order granting jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak house arrest could amount to defying ⁠his decree, a day after authorities delayed Najib’s transfer.
The 73-year-old Najib was jailed for his role in one of the largest-ever global plunders of a sovereign wealth fund, the now-defunct 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).

But King Sultan Ibrahim granted him a conditional pardon in September, allowing him to serve out the rest of his sentence at home provided he paid a $12m fine.
On Friday, thecountry’s attorney general blockedthe former prime minister’s transfer to house arrest after the fine was paid, saying his office needed more clarification on the pardon.
The king said on Saturday there was nothing to clarify, calling the pardon “clear, evident and without any ambiguity”.
“There should be no confusion in interpretation,” King Ibrahim said in a statement, adding it was not tied to any other cases against the former leader.
“Given that all conditions in the conditional pardon order have been fulfilled, any argument questioning the order leads towards denying the order of His Majesty the King.”
Najib’s lawyers thanked the monarch on Saturday, saying there was “no basis” for authorities to keep Najib in prison “a moment longer”.
“They must transfer him immediately to his residence at Jalan Langgak Duta to serve his house arrest, as His Majesty has ordered,” lawyer Farhan Shafee said in a statement.
The Attorney General’s Office issued its own statement shortly afterwards, denying it was challenging the king’s authority while giving no indication if it intended to immediately release Najib.
“This step is not aimed at delaying or denying the implementation of the Conditional Pardon Order, but to avoid any conflict in the implementation of the orders in force and to ensure no sentence is implemented unlawfully,” it said.
Hours later, the prime minister’s office said the attorney general was seeking an audience with the king to “seek pardon” and express an intent to comply, while insisting that legal questions remained that only a court could decide.
The house arrest order applies only to Najib’s first conviction.
He faces ⁠an additional 15 years in prison after being found guilty last year in another 1MDB-linked case, with the sentence set to begin after his stint in ⁠house arrest ends. Najib is appealing the verdict.
The king, a position held in rotation by Malaysia’s nine regional sultans, plays a largely ceremonial role but has the authority to grant pardons ‌under ‌discretionary powers granted by Malaysia’s constitution.
Malaysians hold the monarch and the country’s other sultans in deep respect. Negative remarks about the royalty can be prosecuted under the colonial-era Sedition Act.
